@"/Users/kennywang/Downloads/Take-Home Assignment — Content Intake Pipeline.pdf" I have a pdf with all of the takehome instructions and then a md file detailing how I want this task implemented. # Implementation Brief — Content Intake Pipeline This is a working brief for a take-home assignment. It restates the fixed contract you must build to, and marks the places where a human decision is required before you write code. ## How to use this file 1. Read the whole thing before writing anything. 2. Stop at **Section 0** and get the seven open decisions answered by the human. Do not invent them. They are the primary graded artifact and will be defended in a live session. 3. Build M1 first, end to end, and prove it runs. Then M2. 4. Record decisions in `DECISIONS.md` as they are made, not retroactively. Anything below marked **FIXED** is a contract from the assignment and may not be renamed, restructured, or omitted. Anything marked **OPEN** is a design choice. --- ## Section 0 — Decisions required before coding Do not proceed past this section until each has an answer recorded in `DECISIONS.md`. Where an answer is missing, ask rather than assume. | ID | Decision | Tensions to resolve | |------|----------|---------------------| | D-01 | Work distribution and tracking | How work is assigned and owned; how abandoned work becomes runnable again; how progress is reported. Ownership and state must be durable, not in-process. | | D-02 | Identity and repeated content | Item vs content identifiers; what happens when identical bytes arrive again. Constraint: duplicates never collapse into one item, and no cache entry crosses tenants. A repeat annotation is waste, not an error. | | D-03 | Storage and query paths | Where run state, metadata, extracted text, and annotations live; which store the query surface reads. Durable state must be in Postgres; other stores may sit alongside if they run locally. | | D-04 | Terminal failures | The terminal state model, retryable vs non-retryable, and the machine-readable reason codes consumers see. State names are yours. | | D-05 | Failure semantics at the stub boundary | Timeouts, retry limits, backoff, retryable status codes, terminal outcome when annotation never succeeds. Must account for the window where a call is billed but not durably recorded. | | D-06 | Secondary performance thresholds | Any thresholds you add for throughput degradation, retry amplification, or completion time. Must be defined in advance and must not redefine a mandatory failed condition as a pass. | | D-07 | Local-environment fidelity | Which production behaviors the local environment reproduces, simulates, or leaves untested, and how those gaps affect the evidence. | Also decide up front, and record with its own ID: - Language and runtime. Must be defensible in production. Everything runs on a clean laptop with Docker plus one language runtime. - The two hardest structural problems, which the decisions above must actually answer: - **A global in-flight cap of 2 enforced across four separate OS processes**, with no supervisor and no shared memory. Four independent workers must not collectively exceed the stub's capacity, and `over_capacity_calls` must be exactly zero in the M2 scenario. - **Billed-but-not-recorded.** A worker can be SIGKILLed after the stub has billed a call and before the result is durably stored. The assignment states exactly-once billing is out of scope. Measure and explain duplicate billing; do not claim it is impossible. --- ## Section 1 — What gets built Four components: 1. **Corpus generator** — deterministic generator of test corpora. Source under `src/`. 2. **Annotation stub** — a separately deployed HTTP service simulating a slow, flaky, capacity-limited, billed external dependency. HTTP only. Never imported as a library by the pipeline. 3. **Content intake pipeline** — processes corpora, makes results queryable. 4. **Test harness** — demonstrates behavior under load and failure. Terms, used precisely: - **Tenant** — one customer. Tenants share the pipeline and nothing else. No content, extracted data, annotation, or cache entry crosses between them. - **Corpus** — one generated set of files belonging to one tenant. The unit of submission. - **Run** — one pass over one corpus, identified by a run ID. Submitting the same corpus twice creates two runs over the same bytes. - **Worker** — the unit of concurrency. In-process threads, tasks, or coroutines in M1. Separate, independently killable OS processes in M2. A run processes every file in its corpus: reads its bytes, extracts text and metadata where applicable, calls the stub over HTTP when the item is processable, and durably stores a result that is queryable before the run finishes. --- ## Section 2 — Ground rules (FIXED) - One submission folder with the exact layout in Section 8. All source under `src/`. The four required Markdown files at the root. - The command interface in Section 2a is fixed. - Runs on a clean laptop: Docker plus one language runtime. Everything else starts from your scripts. Prerequisites in the README. - Durable state in Postgres, in a container. - **No external network access at evaluation time.** Setup may download; the running system may not. Vendor or pin anything needed at runtime. - The stub is a remote dependency: HTTP only. - M1 and M2 are both required. A documented cut reads better than a silent omission but still counts as incomplete. ### Section 2a — The unified command interface (FIXED) One executable, `./intake`, at the repository root. Any wrapper works. Subcommands, flags, and outputs are fixed. Query subcommands print JSON to stdout and exit 0 on success, non-zero on error. | Command | Behavior | |---------|----------| | `./intake corpus --seed --size <50..500> --tenant --out [--force]` | Generate a corpus. `--force` overwrites a non-empty directory. | | `./intake stub [--port

]` | Run the annotation stub in the foreground. Default port 8080. | | `./intake up [--workers ]` | Bring up Postgres, the stub on 8080, your service, and the workers. Default 4. Idempotent. | | `./intake down` | Tear the environment down. | | `./intake reset [--workers ]` | Clean slate in one invocation: equivalent to `down` then `up --workers `. Default 4. No other flags. | | `./intake submit --corpus

--tenant ` | Submit a corpus for a tenant. Print JSON with at least `run_id`. The tenant argument is the trusted tenant context. | | `./intake status --run ` | JSON with at least `run_id`, `tenant`, `states` (state name to item count), `terminal` (boolean: every item terminal). | | `./intake item --tenant --id ` | One item as JSON. Not found or wrong tenant: non-zero exit, no data. | | `./intake items --tenant --run [--state ]` | JSON array of items for the run, same shape as `item`, optionally filtered by state. Wrong tenant: not found. | | `./intake kill-worker [--index ]` | SIGKILL exactly one live worker. Print which. It stays dead; no supervisor restart. | | `./intake scenario` | Run the full M2 scenario and its paired control. Print each assertion with pass/fail and reasons. Exit 0 only if all mandatory assertions pass. Write evidence under `evaluation/raw/`. | Extra subcommands and extra JSON keys are fine. The ones above may not change. `./intake item` must return at least: `item_id`, `run_id`, `tenant`, `state`, `sha256`, `bytes`, `source_path`, plus extracted text and annotation where present, and a machine-readable error for failed items. --- ## Section 3 — Corpus generator (normative) Every property below is a requirement. The reviewers regenerate corpora by running this generator. **Determinism (required).** `(seed, size, tenant)` fully determines the output: byte-identical files and manifest on every run and every machine. File bytes depend only on `(seed, size)`. Tenant enters the manifest and never the file content. A `--verify` flag re-derives a corpus from its manifest's own arguments and diffs every byte on disk. **Layout.** The manifest sits next to `files/`, not inside it. Every path under `files/` is exactly one item. ``` / manifest.json files/ ... ``` | ID | Requirement | |----|-------------| | CORPUS-REQ-1 | Item count is an argument, 50 through 500 inclusive. | | CORPUS-REQ-2 | Mixed types: plain text (`.txt`), structured text (`.json`, `.csv`), and a binary type (`.png`, real PNGs). | | CORPUS-REQ-3 | About one file in ten duplicates another byte for byte (within ±2 of `size/10`), sometimes under a different name but always with the same extension. | | CORPUS-REQ-4 | Two deterministic edge cases, flagged in the manifest. An **empty file**: explicit `empty_content` state or clear equivalent terminal state, with **no annotation request**. A **`.json` file holding PNG bytes** whose declared-type parse fails deterministically: explicit `decode_failed` or clear equivalent terminal state, with **no annotation request**. | | CORPUS-REQ-5 | Tenant is an argument. One corpus belongs to one tenant. M2 needs two corpora on different seeds so their content is independent. | **Manifest.** Top level carries `corpus_id`, the arguments, `totals`, the `edge_cases` index, and a digest over the canonical JSON. Per-file entry: ```json { "order": 137, "path": "edge/malformed.json", "extension": "json", "bytes": 1218, "sha256": "…", "role": "edge_case", "duplicate_of": null, "edge_case": "decode_failed", "expected_outcome": "decode_failed", "expects_annotation": false } ``` `expected_outcome` uses neutral names; the pipeline's own state names are its own choice. `expects_annotation` is `false` for exactly the two edge cases. Note on canonical JSON: the digest must be reproducible across machines, so fix key ordering, separators, and encoding explicitly rather than relying on defaults. --- ## Section 4 — Per-item contract Asserted item by item in review, regardless of architecture. | ID | Requirement | |----|-------------| | ITEM-REQ-1 | A stable item ID for the life of the item, plus a cryptographic hash of its bytes. | | ITEM-REQ-2 | Extracted text where the declared type carries text. Type comes from the extension; byte-sniffing is not required. | | ITEM-REQ-3 | Basic metadata: byte size, source path, corpus identifier, tenant, run ID. | | ITEM-REQ-4 | One successful annotation from the stub for every item that reaches annotation. An item ending in a pre-annotation terminal error must not issue an annotation request. | | ITEM-REQ-5 | A terminal state saying what happened, with a machine-readable reason for every unsuccessful item, including declared-type decode failures. | Two traps worth stating plainly: - **PNGs still get annotated.** `expects_annotation` is false for exactly the two edge cases. Everything else, including every binary PNG, reaches annotation. The stub takes raw bytes, so "no extractable text" is not grounds to skip the call. - **The empty file and the fake JSON must terminate before annotation.** Ordering matters: detect these conditions before the HTTP call. Issuing a request for them is a spec violation, not merely wasted spend. --- ## Section 5 — Annotation stub (normative) A separately deployed HTTP process. Its operational behavior is real (latency, failures, capacity, billing all happen at the HTTP boundary) while its answer is simulated: a deterministic function of the request bytes alone. Run as a **single process with a single server worker**. Counters and the failure schedule are per-process state. ### Wire format ``` POST /v1/annotate Content-Type: application/json {"content_b64": ""} ``` `content_b64` is the only accepted field. Any other key is rejected with `400 invalid_request`, so tenant, run ID, path, filename, extension, and idempotency keys cannot reach the service. The annotation object's fields are yours, but it must include the content's SHA-256 and be stable for a given body. A per-call `meta` object may vary. ### Endpoints | Method | Path | Purpose | |--------|------|---------| | POST | `/v1/annotate` | Annotate raw bytes | | GET | `/v1/stats` | Counters | | POST | `/v1/reset` | Reset counters and sequences; optional flat partial config patch in the body | | GET | `/healthz` | Liveness | ### Responses and billing | Status | `error.code` | Billed | When | |--------|--------------|--------|------| | 200 | — | yes | success | | 500 | `server_error` | yes | failure schedule fired | | 429 | `over_capacity` | yes | in-flight limit reached; never admitted | | 400 | `invalid_request` | no | malformed body or unexpected field | No `Retry-After` is sent on 429 or 500. Backoff is the client's problem (D-05). A server error is returned **after** the configured latency and holds a capacity slot for its full duration. ### Required behavior | ID | Requirement | |----|-------------| | EXT-REQ-1 | Per-call latency is configurable and repeatable: fixed, or jittered from a seed, with the same configuration replaying the same latency sequence. | | EXT-REQ-2 | Server errors follow a configurable, resettable schedule: every Nth billed admitted request returns `failure_status`. This fixes how many failures occur, not which item meets them. | | EXT-REQ-3 | Calls in flight are capped at a configurable number. A request above the cap gets the distinct 429. A call leaves the in-flight set when its response is sent or its caller disconnects. | | EXT-REQ-4 | Every request except protocol errors is billed **before** its outcome is chosen. Success, server error, and over-capacity all increment `billed_calls`. There is no idempotency key. | | EXT-REQ-5 | The annotation for a given request body is stable: a repeat call is billed without changing the answer. | | EXT-REQ-6 | `GET /v1/stats` reports at least `billed_calls`, `current_in_flight`, `max_in_flight` (observed peak, not the configured cap), `server_error_calls`, `over_capacity_calls`. | | EXT-REQ-7 | `POST /v1/reset` clears counters, restarts both deterministic sequences, and accepts an optional flat partial configuration patch using the field names below. | ### Configuration Environment variables at startup (`STUB_` prefix, upper-cased), or via the reset patch. | Field | Default | Requirement | |-------|---------|-------------| | `latency_mode` | `fixed` | EXT-REQ-1; `fixed` or `jitter` | | `latency_ms` | 150 | EXT-REQ-1, used when `latency_mode=fixed` | | `latency_jitter_min_ms` / `latency_jitter_max_ms` | 50 / 250 | EXT-REQ-1, jitter bounds | | `latency_seed` | 20260803 | EXT-REQ-1, seeds the jitter sequence | | `failure_every_n` | 7 | EXT-REQ-2; 0 disables failures | | `failure_status` | 500 | EXT-REQ-2, any 5xx | | `in_flight_capacity` | 2 | EXT-REQ-3 | ### Conformance suite Author `tests/test_stub_conformance.py`: a black-box suite asserting this contract over plain HTTP against the running stub (`STUB_URL`, default `localhost:8080`). It must **never** import pipeline code. It must be green at review. Passing it is necessary, not sufficient. --- ## Section 6 — M1, working pipeline (required) Deliverables: the stub, a conforming generator behind `./intake corpus`, a pipeline that runs a corpus end to end through `./intake`, `DECISIONS.md`, and a flowchart in `ARCHITECTURE.md` (components, data movement, durable state, work handoffs; Mermaid, ASCII, or an image) kept current through M2. | ID | Requirement | |----|-------------| | REQ-1.1 | `./intake submit` submits a generated corpus for a tenant and returns a run ID. Every file becomes one item that reaches a terminal state. The two edge cases get exactly their specified outcomes without stopping the run. | | REQ-1.2 | The query surface serves one item by ID and a run's items by state, with every item carrying its tenant and **every read and write scoped to that tenant**. | | REQ-1.3 | An item's result becomes queryable while the rest of the run is still processing. | | REQ-1.4 | Several items are processed at once with configurable concurrency. Workers may live inside a single process in M1, but **item ownership and state must be held in durable storage**. | REQ-1.4 is the M1 requirement that determines whether M2 is achievable. In-process ownership will work in M1 and fail the moment a worker is SIGKILLed. Build the durable ownership model now. --- ## Section 7 — M2, robustness (required) Demonstrate behavior when overlapping load, a degraded dependency, and worker loss land together. One scenario run for real against a paired control, with unfavorable results reported as plainly as favorable ones. ### Required evaluation profile (FIXED) | Setting | Required value | |---------|----------------| | First corpus | Tenant `tenant-a`, 500 items | | Second corpus | Tenant `tenant-b`, 400 items, generated from a different seed | | Workers | Four independently killable OS worker processes | | Submission timing | Submit the second corpus while at least 25% of the first run's items remain nonterminal | | Execution isolation | Each execution starts from empty pipeline state, or a fresh isolated database/namespace, with stub counters and sequences reset. No content or annotation records reused between executions. | | Recorded configuration | Retry limits, timeouts, backoff, and any queue or lease timing, in the report | ### Scenario configuration | Execution | Stub latency | Server failures | In-flight capacity | Injected difference | |-----------|--------------|-----------------|--------------------|---------------------| | Paired control | Fixed 150 ms | Every 7th billed request returns a server error | 2 | No worker is killed | | Fault execution | Fixed 150 ms | Every 7th billed request returns a server error | 2 | Kill one worker | The stub is degraded in **both** executions. The kill is the only difference, which is what makes the billed-call delta attributable. ### Requirements | ID | Requirement | |----|-------------| | REQ-2.1 | Workers run as four independently killable OS processes. `./intake up` brings up the complete local environment; `./intake down` tears it down. | | REQ-2.2 | `./intake scenario` runs the scenario, injects the fault, and prints pass or fail with reasons, asserting all four: (a) the killed worker owned a nonterminal item and stays dead unreplaced; (b) its work resumes elsewhere **within 10 seconds** and every item terminates; (c) one shared limit holds across all workers (`max_in_flight <= 2`, `over_capacity_calls == 0`); (d) retries follow the documented policy and the counters reconcile with item outcomes. | | REQ-2.3 | The scenario overlaps two runs from two tenants on the profile's submission timing, **proven in the output**: each run reaches a terminal item while the other still has nonterminal items, the fault lands while both do, every item is attributed to the correct run and tenant, and cross-tenant lookups return not found (negative test included). | | REQ-2.4 | Run the paired control with the kill as the only difference, each execution from empty pipeline state with the stub reset. Report billed calls for both, the delta, and its explanation. | ### M2 deliverables - Environment scripts, fault injection, profile configuration, assertions, and scenario runner behind `./intake up|down|scenario|kill-worker`. - `EVALUATION.md` summarizing both executions: configuration, verdict, every mandatory assertion, wall-clock time, items per second, attempts, retries, terminal-state counts, recovery timing, stub statistics. - Raw logs and machine-readable results under `evaluation/raw/`, filenames mapping to the summaries, including at least run IDs, start and finish times, per-state item totals, attempt and retry totals, time from kill to recovered processing, and all EXT-REQ-6 statistics. - For every failed condition: state whether it is an expected limitation, a scope cut, or a defect, and what you would change. **An explained failure still fails.** Do not soften a failed assertion into a pass. The 10-second recovery bound is a hard number. Whatever mechanism reclaims abandoned work must be tuned so recovery lands inside it, and the timing must be recorded, not asserted. --- ## Section 8 — Submission layout (FIXED) ``` / ├── intake the ./intake entrypoint (executable) ├── README.md prerequisites, setup, seed/size/tenant per reported run, │ query examples, scope cuts and known defects ├── DECISIONS.md decision log ├── ARCHITECTURE.md current flowchart and design notes ├── EVALUATION.md scenario summary, assertions, metrics, verdict, │ billed-call comparison ├── src/ ALL source: generator, stub, pipeline, M2 harness, │ environment definition ├── tests/ │ ├── test_stub_conformance.py stub conformance suite │ └── ... other tests ├── evaluation/ │ └── raw/ raw logs and machine-readable output, control and fault └── traces/ ├── README.md agent and model, per-trace coverage, redactions, │ missing sessions └── ... exported agent transcripts, privacy-redacted ``` Nothing needed to run or judge the submission may live outside this folder. Prefer concise, evidence-backed writing. The README must record the seed, size, and tenant behind every reported run. ### `DECISIONS.md` format ``` | ID | Decision | Why / trade-off | Date | |------|----------|-----------------|------| | D-01 | ... | ... | ... | ``` Use D-01 through D-07 and add further IDs for other significant decisions. Record decisions as they are made. A change gets a new row referencing the old one. A sentence or two per row is enough. --- ## Section 9 — Traces Session traces are submitted where the agent supports export or stores them locally. Reviewers read them for how work was framed, how generated code was reviewed, and how failures were handled. **Dead ends should remain visible.** Before submission, review every trace: remove secrets, personal data, and unrelated proprietary content, replacing them with explicit markers such as `[REDACTED: API token]`. Never silently delete failed approaches. Summarize redactions and omitted sessions in `traces/README.md`. Legitimate privacy redactions are not penalized. Claude Code default location: `~/.claude/projects//.jsonl`. Keep original filenames. --- ## Section 10 — Out of scope - A user interface. The CLI plus any small HTTP API is sufficient. - Authentication, authorization, user management. Tenant scoping is still required, with the CLI-supplied tenant ID as the trusted context. - Format support beyond CORPUS-REQ-2. - Real machine learning. The stub's annotation is simulated. - Cloud deployment, IaC, CI. Discuss in `ARCHITECTURE.md` only where design-relevant. - Full unit-test coverage. The M2 scenario harness is the primary evaluated test surface. - Exactly-once billing across every crash boundary. Measure and explain duplicate billing rather than claiming it is impossible. --- ## Build order 1. Get D-01 through D-07 answered and written down. 2. Stub, plus the conformance suite. Green before anything depends on it. 3. Generator, plus `--verify`. Determinism proven by re-derivation, not by inspection. 4. Schema and durable ownership model (D-01, D-03). 5. Pipeline with in-process concurrency, driven through `./intake submit`. M1 assertions pass. 6. Convert workers to OS processes; `up`, `down`, `reset`, `kill-worker`. 7. Shared in-flight limiting across processes. 8. Scenario runner, control execution, evidence output. 9. The four Markdown documents, written against what actually happened. ## Standing instructions - Every claim in `EVALUATION.md` traces to a file under `evaluation/raw/`. Do not write a number that is not backed by recorded output. - Do not tune the assertions to make the scenario pass. If an assertion fails, report it as failed and classify it. - Prefer the smallest design that meets the requirements. The reviewers examine scope control. - When a requirement is genuinely ambiguous, pick a reading, record the assumption in `DECISIONS.md`, and build to it. Do not silently resolve ambiguity. - Flag anything built that the human has not reviewed and understood. The submission is defended live. Start by reviewing both documents throughly then lets implement, make sure to go over every design decision with me.

Record decisions in `DECISIONS.md` as they are made, not retroactively. Anything below marked **FIXED** is a contract from the assignment and may not be renamed, restructured, or omitted. Anything marked **OPEN** is a design choice. --- ## Section 0 — Decisions required before coding Do not proceed past this section until each has an answer recorded in `DECISIONS.md`. Where an answer is missing, ask rather than assume. | ID | Decision | Tensions to resolve | |------|----------|---------------------| | D-01 | Work distribution and tracking | How work is assigned and owned; how abandoned work becomes runnable again; how progress is reported. Ownership and state must be durable, not in-process. | | D-02 | Identity and repeated content | Item vs content identifiers; what happens when identical bytes arrive again. Constraint: duplicates never collapse into one item, and no cache entry crosses tenants. A repeat annotation is waste, not an error. | | D-03 | Storage and query paths | Where run state, metadata, extracted text, and annotations live; which store the query surface reads. Durable state must be in Postgres; other stores may sit alongside if they run locally. | | D-04 | Terminal failures | The terminal state model, retryable vs non-retryable, and the machine-readable reason codes consumers see. State names are yours. | | D-05 | Failure semantics at the stub boundary | Timeouts, retry limits, backoff, retryable status codes, terminal outcome when annotation never succeeds. Must account for the window where a call is billed but not durably recorded. | | D-06 | Secondary performance thresholds | Any thresholds you add for throughput degradation, retry amplification, or completion time. Must be defined in advance and must not redefine a mandatory failed condition as a pass. | | D-07 | Local-environment fidelity | Which production behaviors the local environment reproduces, simulates, or leaves untested, and how those gaps affect the evidence. | Also decide up front, and record with its own ID: - Language and runtime. Must be defensible in production. Everything runs on a clean laptop with Docker plus one language runtime. - The two hardest structural problems, which the decisions above must actually answer: - **A global in-flight cap of 2 enforced across four separate OS processes**, with no supervisor and no shared memory. Four independent workers must not collectively exceed the stub's capacity, and `over_capacity_calls` must be exactly zero in the M2 scenario. - **Billed-but-not-recorded.** A worker can be SIGKILLed after the stub has billed a call and before the result is durably stored. The assignment states exactly-once billing is out of scope. Measure and explain duplicate billing; do not claim it is impossible. --- ## Section 1 — What gets built Four components: 1. **Corpus generator** — deterministic generator of test corpora. Source under `src/`. 2. **Annotation stub** — a separately deployed HTTP service simulating a slow, flaky, capacity-limited, billed external dependency. HTTP only. Never imported as a library by the pipeline. 3. **Content intake pipeline** — processes corpora, makes results queryable. 4. **Test harness** — demonstrates behavior under load and failure. Terms, used precisely: - **Tenant** — one customer. Tenants share the pipeline and nothing else. No content, extracted data, annotation, or cache entry crosses between them. - **Corpus** — one generated set of files belonging to one tenant. The unit of submission. - **Run** — one pass over one corpus, identified by a run ID. Submitting the same corpus twice creates two runs over the same bytes. - **Worker** — the unit of concurrency. In-process threads, tasks, or coroutines in M1. Separate, independently killable OS processes in M2. A run processes every file in its corpus: reads its bytes, extracts text and metadata where applicable, calls the stub over HTTP when the item is processable, and durably stores a result that is queryable before the run finishes. --- ## Section 2 — Ground rules (FIXED) - One submission folder with the exact layout in Section 8. All source under `src/`. The four required Markdown files at the root. - The command interface in Section 2a is fixed. - Runs on a clean laptop: Docker plus one language runtime. Everything else starts from your scripts. Prerequisites in the README. - Durable state in Postgres, in a container. - **No external network access at evaluation time.** Setup may download; the running system may not. Vendor or pin anything needed at runtime. - The stub is a remote dependency: HTTP only. - M1 and M2 are both required. A documented cut reads better than a silent omission but still counts as incomplete. ### Section 2a — The unified command interface (FIXED) One executable, `./intake`, at the repository root. Any wrapper works. Subcommands, flags, and outputs are fixed. Query subcommands print JSON to stdout and exit 0 on success, non-zero on error. | Command | Behavior | |---------|----------| | `./intake corpus --seed --size <50..500> --tenant --out [--force]` | Generate a corpus. `--force` overwrites a non-empty directory. | | `./intake stub [--port

]` | Run the annotation stub in the foreground. Default port 8080. | | `./intake up [--workers ]` | Bring up Postgres, the stub on 8080, your service, and the workers. Default 4. Idempotent. | | `./intake down` | Tear the environment down. | | `./intake reset [--workers ]` | Clean slate in one invocation: equivalent to `down` then `up --workers `. Default 4. No other flags. | | `./intake submit --corpus

--tenant ` | Submit a corpus for a tenant. Print JSON with at least `run_id`. The tenant argument is the trusted tenant context. | | `./intake status --run ` | JSON with at least `run_id`, `tenant`, `states` (state name to item count), `terminal` (boolean: every item terminal). | | `./intake item --tenant --id ` | One item as JSON. Not found or wrong tenant: non-zero exit, no data. | | `./intake items --tenant --run [--state ]` | JSON array of items for the run, same shape as `item`, optionally filtered by state. Wrong tenant: not found. | | `./intake kill-worker [--index ]` | SIGKILL exactly one live worker. Print which. It stays dead; no supervisor restart. | | `./intake scenario` | Run the full M2 scenario and its paired control. Print each assertion with pass/fail and reasons. Exit 0 only if all mandatory assertions pass. Write evidence under `evaluation/raw/`. | Extra subcommands and extra JSON keys are fine. The ones above may not change. `./intake item` must return at least: `item_id`, `run_id`, `tenant`, `state`, `sha256`, `bytes`, `source_path`, plus extracted text and annotation where present, and a machine-readable error for failed items. --- ## Section 3 — Corpus generator (normative) Every property below is a requirement. The reviewers regenerate corpora by running this generator. **Determinism (required).** `(seed, size, tenant)` fully determines the output: byte-identical files and manifest on every run and every machine. File bytes depend only on `(seed, size)`. Tenant enters the manifest and never the file content. A `--verify` flag re-derives a corpus from its manifest's own arguments and diffs every byte on disk. **Layout.** The manifest sits next to `files/`, not inside it. Every path under `files/` is exactly one item. ``` / manifest.json files/ ... ``` | ID | Requirement | |----|-------------| | CORPUS-REQ-1 | Item count is an argument, 50 through 500 inclusive. | | CORPUS-REQ-2 | Mixed types: plain text (`.txt`), structured text (`.json`, `.csv`), and a binary type (`.png`, real PNGs). | | CORPUS-REQ-3 | About one file in ten duplicates another byte for byte (within ±2 of `size/10`), sometimes under a different name but always with the same extension. | | CORPUS-REQ-4 | Two deterministic edge cases, flagged in the manifest. An **empty file**: explicit `empty_content` state or clear equivalent terminal state, with **no annotation request**. A **`.json` file holding PNG bytes** whose declared-type parse fails deterministically: explicit `decode_failed` or clear equivalent terminal state, with **no annotation request**. | | CORPUS-REQ-5 | Tenant is an argument. One corpus belongs to one tenant. M2 needs two corpora on different seeds so their content is independent. | **Manifest.** Top level carries `corpus_id`, the arguments, `totals`, the `edge_cases` index, and a digest over the canonical JSON. Per-file entry: ```json { "order": 137, "path": "edge/malformed.json", "extension": "json", "bytes": 1218, "sha256": "…", "role": "edge_case", "duplicate_of": null, "edge_case": "decode_failed", "expected_outcome": "decode_failed", "expects_annotation": false } ``` `expected_outcome` uses neutral names; the pipeline's own state names are its own choice. `expects_annotation` is `false` for exactly the two edge cases. Note on canonical JSON: the digest must be reproducible across machines, so fix key ordering, separators, and encoding explicitly rather than relying on defaults. --- ## Section 4 — Per-item contract Asserted item by item in review, regardless of architecture. | ID | Requirement | |----|-------------| | ITEM-REQ-1 | A stable item ID for the life of the item, plus a cryptographic hash of its bytes. | | ITEM-REQ-2 | Extracted text where the declared type carries text. Type comes from the extension; byte-sniffing is not required. | | ITEM-REQ-3 | Basic metadata: byte size, source path, corpus identifier, tenant, run ID. | | ITEM-REQ-4 | One successful annotation from the stub for every item that reaches annotation. An item ending in a pre-annotation terminal error must not issue an annotation request. | | ITEM-REQ-5 | A terminal state saying what happened, with a machine-readable reason for every unsuccessful item, including declared-type decode failures. | Two traps worth stating plainly: - **PNGs still get annotated.** `expects_annotation` is false for exactly the two edge cases. Everything else, including every binary PNG, reaches annotation. The stub takes raw bytes, so "no extractable text" is not grounds to skip the call. - **The empty file and the fake JSON must terminate before annotation.** Ordering matters: detect these conditions before the HTTP call. Issuing a request for them is a spec violation, not merely wasted spend. --- ## Section 5 — Annotation stub (normative) A separately deployed HTTP process. Its operational behavior is real (latency, failures, capacity, billing all happen at the HTTP boundary) while its answer is simulated: a deterministic function of the request bytes alone. Run as a **single process with a single server worker**. Counters and the failure schedule are per-process state. ### Wire format ``` POST /v1/annotate Content-Type: application/json {"content_b64": ""} ``` `content_b64` is the only accepted field. Any other key is rejected with `400 invalid_request`, so tenant, run ID, path, filename, extension, and idempotency keys cannot reach the service. The annotation object's fields are yours, but it must include the content's SHA-256 and be stable for a given body. A per-call `meta` object may vary. ### Endpoints | Method | Path | Purpose | |--------|------|---------| | POST | `/v1/annotate` | Annotate raw bytes | | GET | `/v1/stats` | Counters | | POST | `/v1/reset` | Reset counters and sequences; optional flat partial config patch in the body | | GET | `/healthz` | Liveness | ### Responses and billing | Status | `error.code` | Billed | When | |--------|--------------|--------|------| | 200 | — | yes | success | | 500 | `server_error` | yes | failure schedule fired | | 429 | `over_capacity` | yes | in-flight limit reached; never admitted | | 400 | `invalid_request` | no | malformed body or unexpected field | No `Retry-After` is sent on 429 or 500. Backoff is the client's problem (D-05). A server error is returned **after** the configured latency and holds a capacity slot for its full duration. ### Required behavior | ID | Requirement | |----|-------------| | EXT-REQ-1 | Per-call latency is configurable and repeatable: fixed, or jittered from a seed, with the same configuration replaying the same latency sequence. | | EXT-REQ-2 | Server errors follow a configurable, resettable schedule: every Nth billed admitted request returns `failure_status`. This fixes how many failures occur, not which item meets them. | | EXT-REQ-3 | Calls in flight are capped at a configurable number. A request above the cap gets the distinct 429. A call leaves the in-flight set when its response is sent or its caller disconnects. | | EXT-REQ-4 | Every request except protocol errors is billed **before** its outcome is chosen. Success, server error, and over-capacity all increment `billed_calls`. There is no idempotency key. | | EXT-REQ-5 | The annotation for a given request body is stable: a repeat call is billed without changing the answer. | | EXT-REQ-6 | `GET /v1/stats` reports at least `billed_calls`, `current_in_flight`, `max_in_flight` (observed peak, not the configured cap), `server_error_calls`, `over_capacity_calls`. | | EXT-REQ-7 | `POST /v1/reset` clears counters, restarts both deterministic sequences, and accepts an optional flat partial configuration patch using the field names below. | ### Configuration Environment variables at startup (`STUB_` prefix, upper-cased), or via the reset patch. | Field | Default | Requirement | |-------|---------|-------------| | `latency_mode` | `fixed` | EXT-REQ-1; `fixed` or `jitter` | | `latency_ms` | 150 | EXT-REQ-1, used when `latency_mode=fixed` | | `latency_jitter_min_ms` / `latency_jitter_max_ms` | 50 / 250 | EXT-REQ-1, jitter bounds | | `latency_seed` | 20260803 | EXT-REQ-1, seeds the jitter sequence | | `failure_every_n` | 7 | EXT-REQ-2; 0 disables failures | | `failure_status` | 500 | EXT-REQ-2, any 5xx | | `in_flight_capacity` | 2 | EXT-REQ-3 | ### Conformance suite Author `tests/test_stub_conformance.py`: a black-box suite asserting this contract over plain HTTP against the running stub (`STUB_URL`, default `localhost:8080`). It must **never** import pipeline code. It must be green at review. Passing it is necessary, not sufficient. --- ## Section 6 — M1, working pipeline (required) Deliverables: the stub, a conforming generator behind `./intake corpus`, a pipeline that runs a corpus end to end through `./intake`, `DECISIONS.md`, and a flowchart in `ARCHITECTURE.md` (components, data movement, durable state, work handoffs; Mermaid, ASCII, or an image) kept current through M2. | ID | Requirement | |----|-------------| | REQ-1.1 | `./intake submit` submits a generated corpus for a tenant and returns a run ID. Every file becomes one item that reaches a terminal state. The two edge cases get exactly their specified outcomes without stopping the run. | | REQ-1.2 | The query surface serves one item by ID and a run's items by state, with every item carrying its tenant and **every read and write scoped to that tenant**. | | REQ-1.3 | An item's result becomes queryable while the rest of the run is still processing. | | REQ-1.4 | Several items are processed at once with configurable concurrency. Workers may live inside a single process in M1, but **item ownership and state must be held in durable storage**. | REQ-1.4 is the M1 requirement that determines whether M2 is achievable. In-process ownership will work in M1 and fail the moment a worker is SIGKILLed. Build the durable ownership model now. --- ## Section 7 — M2, robustness (required) Demonstrate behavior when overlapping load, a degraded dependency, and worker loss land together. One scenario run for real against a paired control, with unfavorable results reported as plainly as favorable ones. ### Required evaluation profile (FIXED) | Setting | Required value | |---------|----------------| | First corpus | Tenant `tenant-a`, 500 items | | Second corpus | Tenant `tenant-b`, 400 items, generated from a different seed | | Workers | Four independently killable OS worker processes | | Submission timing | Submit the second corpus while at least 25% of the first run's items remain nonterminal | | Execution isolation | Each execution starts from empty pipeline state, or a fresh isolated database/namespace, with stub counters and sequences reset. No content or annotation records reused between executions. | | Recorded configuration | Retry limits, timeouts, backoff, and any queue or lease timing, in the report | ### Scenario configuration | Execution | Stub latency | Server failures | In-flight capacity | Injected difference | |-----------|--------------|-----------------|--------------------|---------------------| | Paired control | Fixed 150 ms | Every 7th billed request returns a server error | 2 | No worker is killed | | Fault execution | Fixed 150 ms | Every 7th billed request returns a server error | 2 | Kill one worker | The stub is degraded in **both** executions. The kill is the only difference, which is what makes the billed-call delta attributable. ### Requirements | ID | Requirement | |----|-------------| | REQ-2.1 | Workers run as four independently killable OS processes. `./intake up` brings up the complete local environment; `./intake down` tears it down. | | REQ-2.2 | `./intake scenario` runs the scenario, injects the fault, and prints pass or fail with reasons, asserting all four: (a) the killed worker owned a nonterminal item and stays dead unreplaced; (b) its work resumes elsewhere **within 10 seconds** and every item terminates; (c) one shared limit holds across all workers (`max_in_flight <= 2`, `over_capacity_calls == 0`); (d) retries follow the documented policy and the counters reconcile with item outcomes. | | REQ-2.3 | The scenario overlaps two runs from two tenants on the profile's submission timing, **proven in the output**: each run reaches a terminal item while the other still has nonterminal items, the fault lands while both do, every item is attributed to the correct run and tenant, and cross-tenant lookups return not found (negative test included). | | REQ-2.4 | Run the paired control with the kill as the only difference, each execution from empty pipeline state with the stub reset. Report billed calls for both, the delta, and its explanation. | ### M2 deliverables - Environment scripts, fault injection, profile configuration, assertions, and scenario runner behind `./intake up|down|scenario|kill-worker`. - `EVALUATION.md` summarizing both executions: configuration, verdict, every mandatory assertion, wall-clock time, items per second, attempts, retries, terminal-state counts, recovery timing, stub statistics. - Raw logs and machine-readable results under `evaluation/raw/`, filenames mapping to the summaries, including at least run IDs, start and finish times, per-state item totals, attempt and retry totals, time from kill to recovered processing, and all EXT-REQ-6 statistics. - For every failed condition: state whether it is an expected limitation, a scope cut, or a defect, and what you would change. **An explained failure still fails.** Do not soften a failed assertion into a pass. The 10-second recovery bound is a hard number. Whatever mechanism reclaims abandoned work must be tuned so recovery lands inside it, and the timing must be recorded, not asserted. --- ## Section 8 — Submission layout (FIXED) ``` / ├── intake the ./intake entrypoint (executable) ├── README.md prerequisites, setup, seed/size/tenant per reported run, │ query examples, scope cuts and known defects ├── DECISIONS.md decision log ├── ARCHITECTURE.md current flowchart and design notes ├── EVALUATION.md scenario summary, assertions, metrics, verdict, │ billed-call comparison ├── src/ ALL source: generator, stub, pipeline, M2 harness, │ environment definition ├── tests/ │ ├── test_stub_conformance.py stub conformance suite │ └── ... other tests ├── evaluation/ │ └── raw/ raw logs and machine-readable output, control and fault └── traces/ ├── README.md agent and model, per-trace coverage, redactions, │ missing sessions └── ... exported agent transcripts, privacy-redacted ``` Nothing needed to run or judge the submission may live outside this folder. Prefer concise, evidence-backed writing. The README must record the seed, size, and tenant behind every reported run. ### `DECISIONS.md` format ``` | ID | Decision | Why / trade-off | Date | |------|----------|-----------------|------| | D-01 | ... | ... | ... | ``` Use D-01 through D-07 and add further IDs for other significant decisions. Record decisions as they are made. A change gets a new row referencing the old one. A sentence or two per row is enough. --- ## Section 9 — Traces Session traces are submitted where the agent supports export or stores them locally. Reviewers read them for how work was framed, how generated code was reviewed, and how failures were handled. **Dead ends should remain visible.** Before submission, review every trace: remove secrets, personal data, and unrelated proprietary content, replacing them with explicit markers such as `[REDACTED: API token]`. Never silently delete failed approaches. Summarize redactions and omitted sessions in `traces/README.md`. Legitimate privacy redactions are not penalized. Claude Code default location: `~/.claude/projects//.jsonl`. Keep original filenames. --- ## Section 10 — Out of scope - A user interface. The CLI plus any small HTTP API is sufficient. - Authentication, authorization, user management. Tenant scoping is still required, with the CLI-supplied tenant ID as the trusted context. - Format support beyond CORPUS-REQ-2. - Real machine learning. The stub's annotation is simulated. - Cloud deployment, IaC, CI. Discuss in `ARCHITECTURE.md` only where design-relevant. - Full unit-test coverage. The M2 scenario harness is the primary evaluated test surface. - Exactly-once billing across every crash boundary. Measure and explain duplicate billing rather than claiming it is impossible. --- ## Build order 1. Get D-01 through D-07 answered and written down. 2. Stub, plus the conformance suite. Green before anything depends on it. 3. Generator, plus `--verify`. Determinism proven by re-derivation, not by inspection. 4. Schema and durable ownership model (D-01, D-03). 5. Pipeline with in-process concurrency, driven through `./intake submit`. M1 assertions pass. 6. Convert workers to OS processes; `up`, `down`, `reset`, `kill-worker`. 7. Shared in-flight limiting across processes. 8. Scenario runner, control execution, evidence output. 9. The four Markdown documents, written against what actually happened. ## Standing instructions - Every claim in `EVALUATION.md` traces to a file under `evaluation/raw/`. Do not write a number that is not backed by recorded output. - Do not tune the assertions to make the scenario pass. If an assertion fails, report it as failed and classify it. - Prefer the smallest design that meets the requirements. The reviewers examine scope control. - When a requirement is genuinely ambiguous, pick a reading, record the assumption in `DECISIONS.md`, and build to it. Do not silently resolve ambiguity. - Flag anything built that the human has not reviewed and understood. The submission is defended live. Start by reviewing both documents throughly then lets implement, make sure to go over every design decision with me.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. When calling, specify search breadth: "quick" for a single targeted lookup, "medium" for moderate exploration, or "very thorough" to search across multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- superpowers:brainstorming: You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, or modifying behavior. Explores user intent, requirements and design before implementation.
- superpowers:dispatching-parallel-agents: Use when facing 2+ independent tasks that can be worked on without shared state or sequential dependencies
- superpowers:executing-plans: Use when you have a written implementation plan to execute in a separate session with review checkpoints
- superpowers:finishing-a-development-branch: Use when implementation is complete, all tests pass, and you need to decide how to integrate the work
- superpowers:receiving-code-review: Use when receiving code review feedback, before implementing suggestions, especially if feedback seems unclear or technically questionable - requires technical rigor and verification, not performative agreement or blind implementation
- superpowers:requesting-code-review: Use when completing tasks, implementing major features, or before merging to verify work meets requirements
- superpowers:subagent-driven-development: Use when executing implementation plans with independent tasks in the current session
- superpowers:systematic-debugging: Use when encountering any bug, test failure, or unexpected behavior, before proposing fixes
- superpowers:test-driven-development: Use when implementing any feature or bugfix, before writing implementation code
- superpowers:using-git-worktrees: Use when starting feature work that needs isolation from current workspace or before executing implementation plans - ensures an isolated workspace exists via native tools or git worktree fallback
- superpowers:using-superpowers: Use when starting any conversation - establishes how to find and use skills, requiring skill invocation before ANY response including clarifying questions
- superpowers:verification-before-completion: Use when about to claim work is complete, fixed, or passing, before committing or creating PRs - requires running verification commands and confirming output before making any success claims; evidence before assertions always
- superpowers:writing-plans: Use when you have a spec or requirements for a multi-step task, before touching code
- superpowers:writing-skills: Use when creating new skills, editing existing skills, or verifying skills work before deployment
- anthropic-skills:consolidate-memory: Reflective pass over your memory files — merge duplicates, fix stale facts, prune the index.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers a dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:explain-usage: Explain where this session's tokens went, with one simple chart in plain language. Use when the user says things like "explain my usage", "where did my tokens go", or asks for a usage breakdown.
- anthropic-skills:import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. # Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs

Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.

Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
design, and get your human partner's approval.

<HARD-GATE>
Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any
project, or take any implementation action until you have told your
human partner what you intend and they have approved it. This applies
to EVERY task on EVERY path below — the ceremony scales with the task;
the approval gate never does.
</HARD-GATE>

## Three Paths

Before your first question, classify the request and say the
classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
override it:

- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
  built stays labeled throwaway.
- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Ask the clarifying
  questions that matter, present a short design IN CHAT (a few
  sentences to a few short paragraphs), and STOP. Implementation
  starts only after your human partner says yes to that design — a
  bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an architectural
  one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.

When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.

## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"

Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
artifact, never the approval.

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |

## Checklist

Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
your path and complete them in order.

**Spike:**
1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows
5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway

**Bounded:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
3. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
4. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
5. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document

**Architectural:**
1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
2. **Offer the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, offer it then (its own message); on approval its browser tab opens for you. If no visual question ever arises, never offer it. See the Visual Companion section below.
3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation
5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` and commit
7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
8. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
9. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan

## Process Flow

```dot
digraph brainstorming {
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" [shape=diamond];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [shape=box];
    "Present short design in chat" [shape=box];
    "Human approves?" [shape=diamond];
    "Investigate; report recommendation" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Explore project context" [shape=box];
    "Ask clarifying questions" [shape=box];
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" [shape=box];
    "Present design sections" [shape=box];
    "User approves design?" [shape=diamond];
    "Write design doc" [shape=box];
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" [shape=box];
    "User reviews spec?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke writing-plans skill" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" [shape=box];

    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [label="spike"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [label="bounded"];
    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Explore project context" [label="architectural"];
    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" -> "Human approves?";
    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" -> "Present short design in chat";
    "Present short design in chat" -> "Human approves?";
    "Human approves?" -> "Investigate; report recommendation" [label="spike: yes"];
    "Human approves?" -> "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [label="bounded: yes"];
    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" -> "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural";
    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";
    "Propose 2-3 approaches" -> "Present design sections";
    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";
    "User approves design?" -> "Present design sections" [label="no, revise"];
    "User approves design?" -> "Write design doc" [label="yes"];
    "Write design doc" -> "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)";
    "Spec self-review\n(fix inline)" -> "User reviews spec?";
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Write design doc" [label="changes requested"];
    "User reviews spec?" -> "Invoke writing-plans skill" [label="approved"];
}
```

**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
reported recommendation.

## The Process

The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
is the whole process.

**Understanding the idea:**

- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too
- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria

**Exploring approaches:**

- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design

**Presenting the design:**

- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense

**Design for isolation and clarity:**

- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.

**Working in existing codebases:**

- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.

## After the Design (architectural path)

**Documentation:**

- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
- Commit the design document to git

**Spec Self-Review:**
After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:

1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.

Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.

**User Review Gate:**
After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:

> "Spec written and committed to `<path>`. Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."

Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.

**Implementation:**

- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

## Visual Companion

A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode. Accepting the companion means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.

**Offering the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT offer it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, offer it then, as its own message:
> "This next part might be easier if I show you — I can put together mockups, diagrams, and comparisons in a browser tab as we go. It's still new and can be token-intensive. Want me to? I'll open it for you."

**This offer MUST be its own message.** Only the offer — no clarifying question, summary, or other content. Wait for the user's response. If they accept, start the server with `--open` so their browser opens to the first screen automatically. If they decline, continue text-only and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per-question decision:** Even after the user accepts, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**

- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions

A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.

If they agree to the companion, read the detailed guide before proceeding:
`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`

**Classification: Architectural.** This is a new multi-component system (generator, stub, pipeline, M2 harness) with real distributed-systems problems — durable cross-process work ownership, a shared capacity limit enforced across four independent OS processes with no supervisor, and crash-safe recovery under a 10-second bound. questions.question: D-03: Where should run state, item metadata, extracted text, and annotations live, and what should the query surface (`./intake item`/`items`/`status`) read from?

options.label: Single Postgres, one source of truth (Recommended)

content.text: Now the hardest structural problem — durable work ownership across 4 unsupervised OS processes.

questions.question: D-01: How should work be assigned/owned across 4 independent OS worker processes with no supervisor and no shared memory, and how does an abandoned item (owner SIGKILLed) become runnable again within the 10s recovery bound?

options.label: Postgres lease queue via SELECT...FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (Recommended)
options.description: Each worker atomically claims one pending/expired-lease item with `UPDATE items SET state='in_progress', leased_by=$worker_id, leased_until=now()+lease_dur WHERE id=(SELECT id FROM items WHERE state='pending' OR (state='in_progress' AND leased_until<now()) ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)`. Postgres itself is the coordinator — no separate queue service, no supervisor, works correctly with N racing processes. Lease duration tuned short (~5s) with a periodic reaper query so a killed worker's item becomes claimable well inside 10s. This is the standard, well-understood pattern for exactly this problem.

options.label: Postgres advisory locks per item
options.description: Workers use pg_advisory_lock on item IDs instead of a leased-row pattern. Locks release automatically if the holding connection dies (including on SIGKILL), which elegantly solves abandonment — but advisory locks are session/connection-scoped, so detecting 'this item is stuck' requires polling pg_locks rather than a simple WHERE clause, and combining it with the global in-flight-cap-of-2 (a separate, unrelated resource) adds an extra coordination mechanism rather than reusing one.

content.text: The lease-queue pattern solves item ownership. But there's a second, distinct problem the brief calls out explicitly: the stub allows only 2 concurrent calls total, and that limit must hold across all 4 workers with no supervisor or shared memory — this isn't the same mechanism as item ownership, since a worker can *own* an item without necessarily being *mid-HTTP-call* to the stub at any instant.

questions.question: How should the global in-flight-cap-of-2 against the stub be enforced across 4 independent processes, given `over_capacity_calls` must be exactly 0 (we can never even trigger a 429)?

options.label: Postgres row-semaphore: 2 slot rows, short lease + reaper (Recommended)
options.description: A tiny `stub_call_slots` table with 2 rows. Before calling the stub, a worker atomically claims a free/expired slot (`UPDATE ... WHERE held_by IS NULL OR lease_until<now() ... RETURNING`), releases it right after the call completes. Reuses the exact same lease+reaper primitive as the D-01 item queue — one mechanism, two uses. Lease TTL tuned tight (a few seconds, just above worst-case call duration) so a SIGKILLed worker's slot frees up fast and deterministically.

options.label: Postgres advisory locks (2 fixed lock IDs) held for the call's duration
options.description: Worker holds a dedicated connection, takes `pg_advisory_lock` on one of 2 fixed IDs, releases after the call; Postgres auto-releases the lock if the connection dies. Elegant in theory, but Postgres only notices a SIGKILLed client's connection is dead once the *server-side* TCP stack detects it — without aggressively tuned keepalives this can take far longer than 10 seconds, which risks blowing the recovery bound. Avoidable, but it's an extra fragile knob rather than a deterministic timer.

content.text: Now identity and content-repeat handling.

questions.question: D-02: How should item identity and duplicate-content bytes be handled? (Constraint: duplicates never collapse into one item; no cache entry crosses tenants; a repeat annotation is waste, not an error.)

options.label: UUID item_id per file + per-tenant annotation cache keyed by sha256 (Recommended)
options.description: Every file path gets its own item_id (UUID) regardless of byte content — duplicates stay distinct items, satisfying the hard constraint. Separately, an `annotations` table keyed by (tenant_id, sha256) with a unique constraint stores one annotation per unique content-per-tenant. Before calling the stub, an item checks this cache first; on a hit, it reuses the annotation and skips the HTTP call entirely — turning the ~10% duplicate-content rate into real avoided cost rather than 'harmless but wasteful' repeat billing. Cross-tenant isolation is structural (cache key includes tenant_id).

options.label: UUID item_id per file, no caching — always call the stub
options.description: Same item identity model, but skip the optimization: every item calls the stub even if another item in the same tenant already has that exact content annotated. Simpler (one less table, no cache-hit logic to get right), and still fully spec-compliant since EXT-REQ-5 already guarantees repeat calls are billed-but-harmless. Costs real billed calls on the ~10% duplicate rate for no correctness benefit, and gives up a clean demonstration of understanding D-02's own framing ('a repeat annotation is waste').
